questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [mid] a Calendly-style booking service that never double-books a host (netcalendy, astraupskill/02-CONCEPTS.md). Scenario: 300 tenant companies; a sales host in New York publishes a 30-minute intro call and is available Monday to Friday 9:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00 her time; invitees in Sydney, London and São Paulo book from a public link without an account; her link goes out in a newsletter and 50 invitees try to take Monday 10:00 within the same second; invitees may cancel up to 24 hours before the call; and New York switches to daylight saving time in March. Write your design before you look: how weekly availability becomes concrete bookable slots and in which time zone each step happens, what is stored for a booking, what the create path checks before it accepts a start time, what stops two of the 50 invitees from both getting Monday 10:00, how a public booker's tenant is determined, and how cancellation works. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Keep availability as weekly rules in the host's own zone and expand them into slots on demand: the schedule holds per-weekday local windows plus a time-zone id, each window is cut into steps of the event's duration, and each local slot start is converted to a UTC instant with the schedule's zone before anything is compared.

[w2] Store instants and convert only at the edges: a booking keeps UTC-offset start and end instants, the host's zone is applied when slots are generated, and the invitee's zone is for display; today the slot list's display string is formatted from the UTC instant, so a Sydney invitee would read UTC clock times unless the client converts.

[w3] Use one overlap rule everywhere: a booking that is not cancelled blocks any range that starts before it ends and ends after it starts, so back-to-back meetings are allowed and a cancelled booking blocks nothing; the slot list and the create path must apply the same test.

[w3] Check the requested start against the slot model, not only against other bookings: the create handler verifies the event's scope, its active state and overlapping bookings, but it never asks whether the start is one of the host's slots, so a direct API call can book 3 a.m. on a Sunday. The command's start must fall inside a rule window on the slot grid.

[w3] Know what the current guard really is: the handler runs an overlap query for the host's non-cancelled bookings and, only when it comes back empty, adds the booking and saves; the query and the insert are separate round trips with no lock between them, so several of the 50 simultaneous requests can each see an empty result and each insert.

[w2] Cancellation is a capability, not a login: each booking carries a random token with a unique index, the invitee presents it to cancel, and cancelling only flips the status, which frees the slot because both the availability check and the overlap query skip cancelled bookings.

[w2] Resolve the tenant from the public link itself, before any lookup: the request pipeline already turns an X-Tenant-Slug header or the subdomain into a tenant id for the request, and the booking must then be checked as one tuple of that tenant, the requested host and the selected event.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — launch week. The 50 newsletter invitees all submit Monday 10:00 within one second; the host's Monday really has two windows (9:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00) and she saves both; a colleague in Sydney opens her own booking page for next week; the very first anonymous invitee from the newsletter submits the booking form; New York's clocks jump forward one night; and an invitee cancels ten minutes before the call, another an hour after it. For each: what does the system do today, what goes wrong, and what is the repair?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The overlap query filters by host, status and range but takes no lock and the table has nothing that refuses a second overlapping row, so several invitees each get a confirmed booking for 10:00, each with its own cancellation token, and the host learns of it in the meeting. Make the database the referee (an overlap constraint or a per-host lock taken before the check) and turn its refusal into the same 'no longer available' answer.

[w2] Saving rules accepts several windows for one weekday, but slot generation takes only the first rule it finds for that day, so the afternoon window is never offered; generate slots from every rule for the day and reject overlapping windows when rules are saved.

[w3] Slots are generated per host-local date, but the bookings that mask them are loaded from UTC midnight of the first date to 23:59:59 UTC of the last; for a Sydney host the first morning's slots fall before that UTC start, so bookings there are never loaded and taken slots are offered as free. Load bookings for the UTC span the generated slots actually cover.

[w3] The tenant the handler uses comes only from a token claim, and an anonymous invitee has no token, so the slug the middleware resolved is never consulted and the handler's forced read of the tenant id fails before any check runs: the documented public booking path errors for every anonymous caller. Feed the slug-resolved tenant to public commands.

[w2] Each slot's local wall time is converted to UTC with the host's zone for that specific date, so 9:00 stays 9:00 local across the change and its UTC instant moves an hour, which is correct; but a window that includes the skipped hour asks the conversion for a local time that does not exist, which throws and fails the whole availability request, and a repeated autumn hour is silently read one way. Decide and test both edge rules.

[w2] Cancel refuses only a booking that is already cancelled, so both the ten-minutes-before and the after-the-meeting cancellations succeed and free a slot that is no use to anyone. The 24-hour rule belongs in the domain operation, compared with the booking's start, with an explicit answer when the window has closed.

[w1] The time rules read the ambient clock even though a date-time provider is registered: booking creation compares the start with the real current time, so a cancellation window or 'not in the past' rule cannot be tested at a fixed instant and boundary tests flake. Inject the clock into every rule that compares with now.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your booking design against the alternatives: expanding rules on demand versus storing one row per future slot, the ways to make a double booking impossible in the database (a unique key on host and start, a range-overlap constraint, a per-host lock, serializable transactions), storing UTC instants versus local wall time plus a zone, a slot grid that steps by the event's duration versus arbitrary starts with buffers, and treating the availability list as a promise versus a hint. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Expanding weekly rules on demand needs no slot table and reflects a rule change at once, at the cost of recomputing every request; one stored row per future slot turns 'take this slot' into a single conditional update of one row, but every change to rules, zone or duration means regenerating and reconciling the future rows.

[w3] Today the bookings table has only plain lookup indexes on (host, start) and (tenant, start). Making host plus start unique works only if every booking sits on one shared grid with one length, and breaks as soon as a host offers 15- and 30-minute events; a range-overlap constraint on host and time span (excluding cancelled rows) states the real invariant in PostgreSQL but must be mapped back to a clean conflict; a per-host lock or serializable transactions keep the check-then-insert code but queue or retry a popular host's burst.

[w2] UTC instants compare and sort trivially and mean the same moment for host and invitee; the recurring '9:00 my time' intent lives in the rules with the zone, so a daylight-saving change or a host moving zones shifts future slots while already booked meetings keep their instant.

[w2] Stepping by the event's own duration from the window start is simple and leaves no fragments for a 30-minute call, but gives no buffer between meetings and wastes the tail of a window: a 50-minute event in a 3-hour window yields three slots and 30 unused minutes. Separate slot interval, buffer and minimum notice cost more rules and more tests.

[w2] The availability list is a snapshot: a slot can be taken between reading the list and submitting, so the create path's conflict answer is the authority and the page should treat 'no longer available' as a normal outcome and refresh; promising the list would need a hold on the slot with an expiry.

[w1] Name the guarantee each layer gives instead of claiming the booking is 'safe': the scope check, the slot-membership check, the overlap guard and the time-zone rules are separate invariants with separate tests.
keyPoints.quote: One precise invariant is easier to verify than an unsupported promise of complete safety.
